```{r}
#Library imports used in this analysis
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
library(modelr)
```

## Objective

The objective of this analysis is to investigate how sustainable
practices in agriculture (no-till, crop rotations, etc.) impact yields
for one of the world’s staple crops, corn, to try and establish a more
definite answer for how much farmers should worry over yield losses when
considering adoption of these sustainable practices. We will do this by
modeling corn yield data with growing practices as factors, to determine
the relationship between yields and practice.

## Hypothesis

Hypothesis: Growing practices related to sustainability have little
effect on corn yields.

## Data Collection

Considering data to use for this project, while the initial instinct may
be to use a large sample of yield data from actual farms and compare
their practices, such a dataset is very difficult to find, as farms,
like any other business, prefer to keep the finer details of their
practices and productivity private. Thus we will settle for the next
best thing; study data intentionally giving corn fields different
treatments of growing practices.

Data is from a National Laboratory for Agriculture and Environment study
analyzing individual controlled corn growing plots via the Iowa State
University from 2007-2021, using different combinations of tilling
methods, crop rotations, growing methods, and silage treatments.

Link to the data:
<https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/thirteen-year-stover-harvest-and-tillage-effects-on-corn-agroecosystem-sustainability-in-i-be5ae>

The files from the study used in this project are ‘Field 70-71
CornYield_2008-2021_ForR_0.csv’ for field treatment and yields data,
‘PRISM_MayTemps.csv’ for annual season temperature data, and
‘Rainfall_AEA.csv’ for daily rainfall data.

## Data Processing

Before we can begin graphing and modelling our data to find trends, we
need to change it to a more usable form. In this case, that means
streamlining our columns down to easily referenced variables, and
separating our data by year in addition to plot number, to make distinct
rows of feature values that we can easily reference later.

### Importing the data

Creating a separate tibble for each dataset

```{r}
field_data = read_csv(file.path("Field 70-71 CornYield_2008-2021_ForR_0.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
temp_data = read_csv(file.path("PRISM_MayTemps.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
rain_data = read_csv(file.path("Rainfall_AEA.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
```

### Rainfall Data

Looking at the data we have, the rainfall data is daily rainfall, but
all our other data is yearly. To fix that we’ll be combining the
rainfall data from April-October for 2008-2020 into season totals, to
align with the yields data we have.

It is worth noting that corn is often planted in mid or late April (if
not in early May) and harvested in early or mid October, so including
all the rainfall data from those months could be excessive. However, we
do not have information from our dataset on the exact date that any
plots were planted or harvested, so we include the entire month’s data
to be thorough.

To do this we will be creating a new tibble for seasonal rain data,
which will have Year and Rainfall columns, with each year’s rainfall
being the total rainfall recorded during the growing season
(April-October) for that year.

```{r}
#Making new seasonal rainfall tibble
seasonal_rain_data = rain_data %>% 
  #Filtering for data usable w/ our crop data, so year within 2008-2020, month within April-October
  filter(Year >= 2008 & Year <= 2020 & Month >= 4 & Month <= 10) %>%
  #Aggregating yearly totals
  group_by(Year) %>% summarize(Rainfall = sum(mm))
```

### Field Data

Now we need to process the plot management and yields data. For basic
processing of this data we will:

To separate biochar into its own column, we will be adding a biochar
column w/ value 4 or 13 based on the values in the EndingCropRotation
column, specifically sub-stringing it for “4” and “13” because there
were only two specific levels of biochar application done for this
study.

```{r}
#Adding biochar column w/ values based on EndingCropRotation column
field_data = field_data %>%
  mutate(
    Biochar = if_else(
      grepl("4", EndingCropRotation),
      4,
      if_else(
        grepl("13", EndingCropRotation),
        13,
        0
      )
    )
  )
```

To adjust the InitialCroppingSystem strings we will again just be using
a sub-string approach, matching to “continuous” for continuous, “twin”
for twin-row and “cover” for cover crops (perennial and annual)

Important: Checking against the lowercase version of
InitialCroppingSystem

```{r}
#Simplifying InitialCroppingSystem values
field_data = field_data %>% 
  mutate(
    InitialCroppingSystem = if_else(
      grepl("continuous", tolower(InitialCroppingSystem)),
      "Continuous",
      if_else(
        grepl("twin", tolower(InitialCroppingSystem)),
        "Twin",
        if_else(
          grepl("cover", tolower(InitialCroppingSystem)),
          "Cover",
          ""
        )
      )
    )
  )
```

Dropping EndingCropRotation, Treatment and Stover Harvest Level columns

```{r}
#Dropping EndingCropRotation, Treatment and Stover Harvest Level columns
field_data = field_data %>% select(
  -starts_with("Stover"), 
  -EndingCropRotation, 
  -Treatment, 
  -Crop2017)
```

Renaming InitialCroppingSystem and EndingCroppingSystem columns

```{r}
#Renaming InitialCroppingSystem and EndingCroppingSystem columns
field_data = field_data %>% 
  rename(
    System = InitialCroppingSystem,
    Rotation = EndingCroppingSystem
  )
```

Replacing NaN in LevelStoverHarvest column with None

```{r}
#Replacing NaN in LevelStoverHarvest column with None
field_data = field_data %>%
  replace_na(
    list(LevelStoverHarvest = "None")
  )
```

### Time-Bounding

Now the most important piece of processing for field data, splitting
between years. For this analysis, we want to treat every plot/year
combination as its own data point, so we will be splitting the rows of
field_data into multiple rows based on year.

To do this we will be making a new tibble crop_data with each row being
a unique year/plot combination. This tibble will also hold rainfall and
temperature information, as these are relevant factors for corn yields.
To accomplish this we will:

Creating crop_data from field_data via pivot

```{r}
#Pivoting field_data into crop_data w/ pivot_longer to make GrainYear by year values
crop_data = field_data %>% pivot_longer(
  cols = starts_with("Grain"),
  names_to = "Year",
  values_to = "Yield",
  names_prefix = "Grain"
)
```

Dropping years w/o yield data

```{r}
#Removing years for which Yield data is missing w/ drop_na
crop_data = crop_data %>% drop_na(Yield)
```

Adding rain and temp data to main tibble crop_data via joins

```{r}
#Making sure all Year fields are set as type double for comparison
crop_data = crop_data %>% mutate(Year = as.double(Year))
seasonal_rain_data = seasonal_rain_data %>% mutate(Year = as.double(Year))
temp_data = temp_data %>% mutate(Year = as.double(Year))

#Joining crop_data and seasonal_rain_data on Year
crop_data = inner_join(crop_data, seasonal_rain_data, by = "Year")

#Joining crop data and temp_data on Year
crop_data = inner_join(crop_data, temp_data, by = "Year")
```

Setting biochar application outside 2013 to 0

```{r}
crop_data = crop_data %>% mutate(
  Biochar = if_else(
    Year == 2013,
    Biochar,
    0
  )
)
```

## Exploratory Analysis [Continuous]

The plots that we will use for this graphing will be violin plots, as
even for our continuous values the values are still sparse, as we only
have unique temp/rainfall/year values for each year. Violin plots are
useful because they allow us to see the distribution of points with the
same x-axis value, something very difficult to see with densely packed
data in a scatter plot.

For biochar application, we will only graph continuous corn plots in
2013 because biochar was only applied to continuous corn fields in 2013.
We will get just the continuous corn plot data by filtering on the value
of the Rotation column (in addition to filtering on Year).

### Corn Yields over Time

```{r}
#Violin Plot
ggplot(data=crop_data, aes(x = factor(Year), y = Yield)) +
  geom_violin() + 
  labs(
    title = "Corn Yields over Time",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Corn Yields (Bushels per Acre)"
  )
```

```{r}
#Summary Statistic Tibble
year_avgs = crop_data %>% group_by(Year) %>% summarize(Yield = mean(Yield))
print(year_avgs)
```

### Corn Yields w/ Rainfall

```{r}
#Violin Plot
ggplot(data=crop_data, aes(x = factor(Rainfall), y = Yield)) +
  geom_violin() + 
  labs(
    title = "Corn Yields w/ Rainfall",
    x = "Rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Corn Yields (Bushels per Acre)"
  )
```

```{r}
#Summary Statistic Tibble
rain_avgs = crop_data %>% group_by(Rainfall) %>% summarize(Yield = mean(Yield))
print(rain_avgs)
```

### Corn Yields w/ Biochar Application

Limited to year 2013 and continuous corn plots, the only plots biochar
was applied to

```{r}
#Violin Plot
ggplot(data=filter(crop_data, Year==2013, Rotation=="Continuous Corn"), aes(x = factor(Biochar), y = Yield)) +
  geom_violin() + 
  labs(
    title = "Corn Yields w/ Biochar Application",
    x = "Biochar (Tons per Acre)",
    y = "Corn Yields (Bushels per Acre)"
  )
```

```{r}
#Summary Statistic Tibble
biochar_avgs = filter(crop_data, Year==2013, Rotation=="Continuous Corn") %>% group_by(Biochar) %>% summarize(Yield = mean(Yield))
print(biochar_avgs)
```

Looking at our graphs for yields plotted against continuous values, we
see a bit of an upward trend in yields with rainfall, as one would
expect, but otherwise see little clear relationship with temperature,
presumably owing to the relatively low size of the temperature sample
size, and to that no particularly cold season starts were recorded, the
main factor that could cause temperature to become a significant factor
for corn growth. For biochar, we see little difference in yield with
greater biochar application, likely because fertilizer is applied to the
fields as needed regardless of biochar application, although
unfortunately data on fertilizer application is not available for the
study we are working with.

The lack of yield trend over time is in-line with the study we are
working with, which treated each plot similarly over the course of the
study.

## Exploratory Analysis [Categorical]

again using violin plots. The categorical values of interest for us are
tilling method, crop rotation, growing system and stover harvest level,

column as the x-axis and yield on the y-axis.

Looking at our graphs for categorical values, we see little difference
in yield distributions for different practices. This lack of a trend
would be within itself informative, and we will now move onto building a
model to determine more definitively if the trends we have seen in our
exploratory analysis will hold true.

## Modelling

For this analysis, we will be building a multiple linear regression
model to predict corn yields given information on the climatic
conditions and the growing practices used.

### Choosing Inputs

Our first step will be to identify what input values we want to use. So
far we have analyzed the relationship of corn yields to mean
temperature, low temperature, high temperature, seasonal rainfall,
biochar application, tilling method, crop rotation, growing method and
stover harvest level.

For this model we will be eliminating biochar from consideration as a
variable, as it having only been applied to continuous corn plots in
2013 means the sample size for its application is much lower (making
getting good results harder), and our exploratory analysis indicated
that it had little effect on yields when it was applied.

We will also be using only mean temperature, as the temperature plots we
created in our exploratory analysis showed little difference in
distribution of yields between low, mean and high May temperatures.
Considering that temperature’s effect is not of particular interest to
us given that it is not a component of farm management but rather just
an environmental factor, we will be using just mean temperature to
represent temperature to simplify its implementation in our model. This
will hopefully allow us to gather more meaning on the effect of
cultivation practices on corn yields, our goal for this project.

This leaves us with an input factor set of mean temperature, seasonal
rainfall, tilling method, crop rotation, growing method and stover
harvest level.

### Encoding Categorical Values as Factors

To do regression we need R to treat our categorical variables as
categories rather than numbers. Converting them to factors lets lm()
automatically dummy-code them (one 0/1 indicator per non-reference
level), so the model estimates a separate effect for each practice
relative to a baseline, without assuming the levels are ordered or
evenly spaced.

The first level listed for each factor is the baseline the other levels
are compared against, chosen here as the conventional practice:

```{r}
#Converting categorical columns to factors for regression
#Doing so in a copy of crop_data to preserve base data
#Also removing fields not used in model 
#(PlotNo, Field, Block, Biochar, Low Temp, High Temp)
model_data = crop_data %>% mutate(
  Tillage = factor(Tillage, levels = c("Chisel", "No-till")),
  LevelStoverHarvest = factor(LevelStoverHarvest, levels = c("None", "Moderate", "High")),
  System = factor(System, levels = c("Continuous", "Twin", "Cover")),
  Rotation = factor(Rotation, levels = c("Continuous Corn", "Corn-Alfalfa", "Cover Crop"))
) %>%
  select(-PlotNo, -Field, -Block, -Biochar, -May.tmin.C, -May.tmax.C)
```

### Leave-One-Year-Out Modeling

For each selected year from 2008 through 2020, that entire year is held
out for evaluation, and the models are trained on all other available
years in the dataset (rather than only on earlier years). The RMSE and
R-squared are reported separately for each held-out year.

```{r}
# Selected evaluation years
selected_years = 2008:2020

# Evaluate the full model year by year, leaving the test year out of training
full_model_results = map_dfr(selected_years, function(test_year) {
  train_data = model_data %>% filter(Year != test_year)
  test_data = model_data %>% filter(Year == test_year)

  yield_model = lm(Yield ~
    LevelStoverHarvest +
    Tillage +
    System +
    Rotation +
    Rainfall +
    May.tmean.C,
    data = train_data)

  predictions = predict(yield_model, newdata = test_data)
  tibble(
    Year = test_year,
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((test_data$Yield - predictions)^2)),
    R2 = 1 - sum((test_data$Yield - predictions)^2) /
      sum((test_data$Yield - mean(test_data$Yield))^2)
  )
})

# Report metrics separately for each evaluation year
full_model_results
full_model_results %>% summarise(avg_RMSE = mean(RMSE), avg_R2 = mean(R2))
```

## Practices Only Model

Similar to the full model, but omits rainfall and temperature as inputs.
Each selected year is evaluated using a model trained on all other
available years, excluding the held-out year.

```{r}
# Evaluate the practices-only model year by year, leaving the test year out of training
practice_model_results = map_dfr(selected_years, function(test_year) {
  train_data = model_data %>% filter(Year != test_year)
  test_data = model_data %>% filter(Year == test_year)

  practice_model = lm(Yield ~
    LevelStoverHarvest +
    Tillage +
    System +
    Rotation,
    data = train_data)

  predictions = predict(practice_model, newdata = test_data)
  tibble(
    Year = test_year,
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((test_data$Yield - predictions)^2)),
    R2 = 1 - sum((test_data$Yield - predictions)^2) /
      sum((test_data$Yield - mean(test_data$Yield))^2)
  )
})

# Report metrics separately for each evaluation year
practice_model_results
practice_model_results %>% summarise(avg_RMSE = mean(RMSE), avg_R2 = mean(R2))
```

Neither model appears to hold much predictive power at all, generally
landing negative on R-squared values except for in select years, where
even the highest values still remain notably low. This at the very least
indicates that these features lack strong predictive power for
predicting yields. And from that, it can reasonably be stated, that they
lack any strong *negative* impact on yields, as that would have yielded
models with literally any predictive power.
